articles.title: Honor the Rosies where they belong: On the National Mall
articles.summary: Each year, there are fewer living Rosies. Those of us left hope to see firsthand the day that our efforts, and our sacrifices, are remembered and honored on the National Mall alongside our memorials commemorating America’s heroes.
articles.body:
I was 17 years old when I first picked up a rivet gun.

It was the summer of 1943, and I had started my first-ever job attaching sheet metal to the frames of airplane wings — mostly B-17s and B-29s, U.S. military aircraft used during the Second World War. The job paid well, but what I remember most is how proud I was to be contributing to the war effort, to something bigger and more important than myself.

Though I didn’t know it at the time, my decision that summer to leave my small North Dakota hometown for Seattle to join The Boeing Co. marked my initiation into an incredible contingent of women with bandanas and can-do attitudes who would one day become American icons.

The “Rosie the Riveters,” or more simply the “Rosies,” are the 18 million American women who answered the call when legions of men across the United States departed to fight the Axis powers. We worked long hours carefully assembling the planes, tanks and ships that would be sent to support the war overseas. But women served in many other roles, keeping America’s entire economic engine running.

They were mechanics, pilots, engineers, electricians, code breakers, autoworkers, lumberjacks, farmers and ranchers — united in their effort to hold down the home front. These often overlooked jobs demonstrated the wide range of responsibilities women took on during the war, helping to reshape perceptions of what women could contribute both in the workforce and in national service.

We didn’t do the work for praise but to save our country and our family members who were overseas. We felt the call to serve just as strongly as the men did. And the women of the Greatest Generation helped secure Allied victory, saved American lives, and strengthened the home front during one of the most consequential periods in our history.

As we celebrate America250 this year, it is a unique opportunity to recognize the Rosies as enduring symbols of civic pride, sacrifice and devotion to the American ideal. The strength of our nation has always depended on ordinary citizens willing to do extraordinary things in service to their country. The Rosies were no exception, embodying the American tradition of service every day they dutifully showed up to work.

In 2024, I was asked to accept the Congressional Gold Medal on behalf of these 18 million women. It was the honor of my lifetime. A memorial on the National Mall would ensure that honor endures for generations to come.

Recognizing the Rosies’ lasting impact on the U.S., Congress passed bipartisan legislation in 2022 authorizing a national memorial to the women who served on the home front during World War II. This memorial will not only honor their service but also educate future generations about the indispensable role women played in securing victory and advancing the cause of freedom.

The effort is now in the site selection and approval phase. And I believe the National Mall, in close proximity to the existing World War II Memorial, is the most fitting and prominent location for telling this important chapter of American history.

There is bipartisan legislation in Congress that would allow just that. The World War II Women’s Memorial Location Act would permit the memorial to be located on or near the National Mall, placing the story of America’s World War II women alongside the memorial honoring the esteemed veterans who fought overseas. Late last year, the House of Representatives passed the World War II Women’s Memorial Location Act with overwhelming bipartisan support. However, the bill is now stalled in the Senate.

I refuse to let that be the end of our story.

Each year, there are fewer living Rosies. Those of us left hope to see firsthand the day that our efforts, and our sacrifices, are remembered and honored on the National Mall alongside our memorials commemorating America’s heroes.

This year, I turned 100 years old. But I remain as determined as I was at 17 when I left home to pick up a rivet gun. So I am calling on the Senate to pass — and President Trump to sign — the World War II Women’s Memorial Location Act. We answered our country’s call when freedom was at stake. Now, I ask our nation to ensure that our story, and the lessons it carries, will never be forgotten.

Mae Krier is an original Rosie the Riveter who worked on Boeing aircraft during World War II, from 1943 to 1945. She helped to establish National Rosie the Riveter Day in 2017 and accepted the Congressional Gold Medal on behalf of all her fellow Rosies in 2024.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia agree to ‘energy ceasefire’
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he was unaware of the deal, but that Ukraine would back it.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has announced what he called an ‘energy ceasefire’ between Ukraine and Russia, after mutual attacks on energy infrastructure piled pressure on global energy prices.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed,” Trump wrote on social media on Sunday. “Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied any knowledge of the agreement and said it was “news to him,” according to Axios.

But he confirmed Ukraine would back the deal, saying in a post on Telegram: “Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side.”

Zelenskyy previously said on Sunday he would organise elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin agrees to a 60-day full ceasefire.

On Saturday, Trump slammed the Ukrainian president for attacking Russian oil refineries, the day after the US temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were originally imposed to sap Moscow’s war effort in Ukraine.

“He better damn well stop,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” he added.

Earlier on Saturday, Zelenskyy said Trump’s announcement of the diesel deal with Putin had emboldened Moscow. Kyiv instead urged Washington to pressure Moscow for serious negotiations to end the four-and-a-half-year war.

“Today, Russia said thank you for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said.

“Last night provided yet more confirmation that Russia perceives any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly keep fighting, that it can supposedly keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”

The southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia has been a regular target of Russian bombardment , with attacks intensifying in the past few months.

On Saturday, a six-year-old girl was among those killed in Zaporizhzhia when one attack reduced part of an apartment block to rubble. Her grandfather, Anatoliy Chumniy, stood sobbing over her body, laid on the ground in a white bag, after rescuers pulled her from the wreckage.

In response to Trump’s suggestion of a new leader, Zelenskyy said, “it’s up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader and noted that Putin would also like to change who is leading Ukraine.

Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceases its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

articles.summary: Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) paid a Kansas bakery $1,300 Saturday after its owner publicly accused his campaign of leaving a nearly $700 bill unpaid for six years. articles.body:
Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) paid a Kansas bakery $1,300 Saturday after its owner publicly accused his campaign of leaving a nearly $700 bill unpaid for six years.

The payment came days after Holly Thomas, owner of Holly’s Sweet Treats in Hutchinson, Kan., said Marshall’s 2020 Senate campaign never paid for cookies, cupcakes and brownies ordered for his Republican primary election watch party.

Marshall said he had no knowledge of the outstanding bill and moved to settle it after learning of Thomas’s claims.

“We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double,” Marshall wrote on social media Saturday.

The senator also shared a screenshot of a digital receipt showing a $1,300 payment to the bakery.

Thomas said Thursday that the campaign had left her with a $678.75 bill at a time when her newly opened business was struggling through the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Do you know why I will never vote for Roger Marshall?” Thomas wrote on Facebook . “Because six years ago, when I was a brand-new small business owner, his campaign ordered cookies and treats from my bakery for his primary election watch party. And I never got paid.”

According to an invoice Thomas shared, the campaign ordered $375 worth of custom sugar cookies, $75 in cupcakes and $175 in fudge brownies.

Thomas said she spent nearly a year trying to collect payment, repeatedly contacting the campaign by phone and email without receiving a response.

“Not only was I just starting out, but we were also in the middle of COVID, when small businesses everywhere were struggling just to keep their doors open. Every single dollar mattered,” she wrote. “Those cookies and treats cost money to make, employees’ time to prepare, and resources that my little business couldn’t afford to give away.”

Marshall, a physician who was first elected to the Senate in 2020, has previously been scrutinized over his medical practice’s efforts to collect unpaid bills from patients. The New York Times uncovered hundreds of debt collection lawsuits involving the practice.

articles.title: Trump, Vance blitz Ohio as Democrats look to flip governor’s mansion
articles.summary: The red-leaning Buckeye State governor’s mansion could flip for the first time in two decades as Democrat Amy Acton narrowly leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in recent polls of their bitter midterm battle. A new CNN poll Thursday showed Acton up 8 percentage points over Ramaswamy, after a New York Times/Siena poll found Acton ahead by…
articles.body:
The red-leaning Buckeye State governor’s mansion could flip for the first time in two decades as Democrat Amy Acton narrowly leads Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in recent polls of their bitter midterm battle.

A new CNN poll Thursday showed Acton up 8 percentage points over Ramaswamy, after a New York Times/Siena poll found Acton ahead by 4 points last week. Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages now show Acton up roughly 4 points, rating the race a toss-up.

The wide-open race to succeed outgoing Gov. Mike DeWine (R) comes against the backdrop of a highly competitive Senate race and a handful of battleground House contests, putting Republicans on defense in races they’ve easily won in recent years.

Ohio is the latest red stronghold in the spotlight of President Trump’s cross-country campaign blitz as he seeks to energize base voters. After Trump rallied outside Dayton for Ramaswamy last weekend, Vice President Vance stopped in Lima on Friday and Trump is headed to Youngstown on Monday to campaign for Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).

“I think Republicans are clearly very concerned about Ohio,” said Justin Buchler, an associate professor of political science at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland.

“There are a set of races that they probably expected to be safer, and they are seeing a few of those races, if not slip away, then certainly look more precarious for them, and you can see that by where Trump and Vance are going.”

Ramaswamy, a biotech entrepreneur who ran for president in 2024, boasts prime endorsements from DeWine, Vance and Trump in his bid for a governor’s mansion that Republicans have held since 2010.

He was a controversial candidate but effusive ally of Trump even as they fought for the GOP’s White House nod last cycle and was later tapped to help lead Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) crackdown on federal spending alongside tech mogul Elon Musk. And with a net worth estimated at $2.3 billion, Ramaswamy has been able to partially self-fund his midterm bid at home in Ohio.

But Republicans across the country face significant midterm headwinds — from Trump’s sunken approval ratings to the historic trend of the ruling party losing out between presidential cycles — and Ramaswamy faces tough competition in Acton.

A physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, Acton worked with DeWine and other Republican leaders as she led the state’s response to the pandemic. Supporters have touted her bipartisan work along the campaign trail, arguing Acton “ will work with anyone .” Like Ramaswamy, she has not held elected office before.

“The governor’s race is very unusual because we have unusual candidates for each party … neither of them are really conventional candidates,” Buchler said.

And with less than a month to go until Election Day, the rivals have been ramping up their attacks.

Acton’s campaign has painted Ramaswamy as an out-of-touch billionaire, while Republican groups have accused Acton of being an alcoholic and drug addict — claims she’s decried as “horrible.” There is currently no scheduled debate between the two candidates.

Meanwhile, the Senate race between Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is also considered a critical toss-up in the fight for control of the upper chamber.

Brown led by 6 points in the CNN polling and by 4 points in The New York Times results, while Husted led by 1 point in a co/efficient survey.

Acton’s campaign manager, Philip Stein, said the numbers are a signal that “Ohioans are ready for a change.”

But Republicans in the state are shaking off the polls and pointing to their past winning streak.

“It’s a Republican state and more red in midterm elections, and that serves Vivek Ramaswamy and John Husted and the Republicans up and down the ticket well,” said Ohio GOP consultant Matt Dole.

“It’s certainly closer — you know, our governor won by 27 points or something like that four years ago — it’s not that type of environment, and certainly the national environment is challenging,” Dole said. “But I think the fundamentals still, despite what the polls say, are advantageous for Republicans.”

Others say a red win is more uncertain as Trump’s approval declines among voters in Ohio, a state where Republicans easily outnumber Democrats.

Robert Alexander, a political science professor at Bowling Green State University in Ohio, said that the tight polls, the ad blitz and “multiple visits from Trump and Vance” signal that “those polls probably aren’t too far off, and that they also expect a very close race.”

Trump “is not what he was certainly two years ago,” Alexander said, which might mean a “backlash effect” from disaffected Republicans or independents frustrated by the status quo.

“The Democrat brand is not as strong in the state as the Republican brand … but the headwinds against Republicans right now are pretty strong.”

After casting his own early ballot Friday in Ohio, Vance urged the crowd in Lima to vote for both Husted and Ramaswamy — saying Republicans “need” Ramaswamy to win “because he is running against a crazy person.” The vice president was notably a senator for Ohio for just two years before he was tapped to join Trump’s presidential ticket.

In Vandalia, Ohio, last weekend, Trump urged supporters to turn out and vote red no matter what.

“Go out and vote. Even if you hate Jon Husted, even if you hate Vivek Ramaswamy, you’re gonna go out, you’re gonna vote, and then you’re gonna pull their triggers,” Trump said.

Amid Trump’s poor approval rating, Ohio Democratic strategist Jeff Rusnak suggested the president’s trip could backfire.

“I think what he’s doing is firing up Democrats and Independents who are really turned off by him and even some of those Republicans who have had enough,” Rusnak said, arguing Trump is “in for a rude awakening” when he talks to voters in the Mahoning Valley on Monday.

But observers on all sides of the aisle agree the Senate and gubernatorial races will come down to turnout, as evidenced by Trump’s call to Ohioans with early and absentee voting already underway .

“Preferences, I think, are leaning toward Democrats in the state this year, but those preferences don’t translate to votes,” Alexander said.

He described a “nightmare scenario” for Republicans in which some voters don’t want Acton or Brown on the Democratic side — but still aren’t “excited” enough about Ramaswamy or Husted in the GOP column.

“It’s cliche to say it all depends on turnout, but that’s the reality, and I think that’s exactly why you’re seeing Trump and Vance come to the state.”

articles.title: WATCH: CDC director discusses US government response to Russian plague concerns: 'We are protected'
articles.summary: CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz says the agency is monitoring travelers from Siberia amid concerns about a pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia.
articles.body: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is coordinating with federal agencies to monitor travelers entering the United States from Siberia amid concerns about a possible pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia, the agency's director revealed Wednesday. CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said the Trump administration is working across multiple agencies to identify travelers arriving from the region following the mysterious death of a Russian laboratory worker, while emphasizing that the risk to Americans remains minimal. "We are very confident that the threat to the United States is extremely low," Schwartz said during a Wall Street Journal health forum Wednesday. MOTHER OF DEAD RUSSIAN ANTI-PLAGUE INSTITUTE WORKER: 'I KNOW THE TRUTH' The concerns stem from the Oct. 2 death of Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, whose death has fueled speculation about a possible pneumonic plague infection. Russian authorities have maintained that Shipilova died from pneumonia of unknown origin and have not confirmed that she was infected with Yersinia pestis, the bacteria that causes pneumonic plague. Schwartz said the CDC is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State and War, among other federal agencies, to track potential arrivals from the region. "There are about 200 flights that come into the United States from Siberia, that region," Schwartz said, adding that those flights typically arrive at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport. "We have a port health station set up in JFK so that we can do appropriate surveillance and screening if anyone from that area comes into the United States," she continued. The CDC director stressed that while pneumonic plague is a serious bacterial infection capable of spreading between people through respiratory droplets, early detection and treatment can prevent deaths. TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP' "The one good thing, if I could say there's a good thing, is that it's a treatable, highly treatable bacterial disease with common antibiotics that most physicians within the United States can utilize," Schwartz said. The illness is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and is considered the most serious form of plague, according to the CDC. Symptoms can include fever, chest pain, coughing and rapidly developing pneumonia. Without prompt antibiotic treatment, the infection can be fatal, the agency warns. The World Health Organization (WHO) has pressed Moscow for additional information about Shipilova's death. Russian authorities placed approximately 200 people who had contact with the deceased laboratory worker under quarantine, according to Euronews. On Thursday, Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said preventive measures had been completed and roughly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no pathogens, according to the Associated Press. RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE ‘FAR WORSE’ THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP However, Russian officials have not publicly identified the pathogen responsible for Shipilova's pneumonia or definitively ruled out pneumonic plague as the cause of her death, according to The Associated Press. Asked whether Moscow was being sufficiently transparent with American authorities, Schwartz indicated that the administration was still seeking answers. "We are still having those conversations about what exactly happened in Siberia," she said, adding that U.S. officials were working with information about an unconfirmed case of pneumonic plague.

articles.title: Rescue expert warns FlyDubai hijacking attempt shows US, allies are ‘playing checkers’ against terror threat

United Arab Emirates investigators have described the incident aboard FlyDubai flight FZ1073 as an attempted terror attack after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and tried to hijack the plane, which was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israelis. I would get 19 hijackers, and I would hijack four airplanes, and I would fly them into buildings in America, and then issue a communique that said: 20 years of war, you are no safer today than you were before – that for TSA, and Homeland Security, and Iraq, and Afghanistan and all the different things, you are actually no safer, America, today than you were before," he said. "We're seeing, sadly," he lamented, "that academic hypothetical situation has now become a reality, or certainly a possibility." Despite President Donald Trump and the War Department's best efforts to rid the world of terrorist groups – and Iran of nuclear weapons aspirations – "you can't bomb your way into peace," Stern claimed. 'CRAZY' FLYDUBAI LANDING EXPLAINED BY ISRAELI PILOT, WHO OFFERS STEPS TO PREVENT FUTURE CRISES "They have been in holy war against us," he added. "We have now engaged in a holy war against them." "On Ramadan, the holiest month of the year in Islam, on the first day, which is the holiest day, we detonated the leader of the Shia faith, the Ayatollah," he said, likening it to "if somebody assassinated the pope on Easter Sunday while he's giving mass at the Vatican." Stern explained that rooting out ideological terror in the U.S. is more complex than ever, because even if the border is not open any longer under Trump, the terrorist networks might be infiltrating America with U.S. passport holders – making them tough to investigate, if not impossible to spot before an attack. Stern noted that the nature of America's adversaries in the current conflict is unlike what the U.S. faced in places like Afghanistan. IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY "The Persian Empire is the only empire of empires who have been all the way on top and all the way defeated at the bottom – six times," he said. Stern predicted that some day even 9/11 — which he survived as a first responder — is ultimately going to be dwarfed. articles.title: AP source: Trump, Rubio weigh firing U.S. envoy to Greece after mounting reports of improper conduct
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.

A senior U.S. official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday's Columbus Day holiday.

The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled.

In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.

Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the U.S. embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her.

After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.

The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied.

A second U.S official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.

The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.

The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.

The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.

Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.

Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.

Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr.

articles.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan t...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to "immediately reverse course" on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.

Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.

The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.

Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.

"We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied," Tillis said.

Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.

The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.

"Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies," the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law."

Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law.

"The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said on CBS's "Face the Nation."

He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.

"This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world," Barrasso said.

Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices.

articles.title: Prominent Republican senator says Trump's Russian diesel deal may be illegal
articles.summary: By Jan Wolfe Oct 11 (Reuters) - Republican US Senator Thom Tillis on Sunday said President Donald Trump's diesel supply ​deal with Russia may be illegal and...
articles.body:
Oct 11 (Reuters) - Republican US Senator Thom Tillis on Sunday said President Donald Trump's diesel supply deal with Russia may be illegal and will put American lives at risk, adding to bipartisan criticism of the arrangement announced by the president on Friday.

Trump ‌said that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel that were designed ‌to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.

"I do believe there's a legitimate case for saying the president's not following the law," Tillis, an influential Republican from North Carolina who ​is retiring from the Senate at the end of his term in January, told NBC's "Meet the Press" with Kristen Welker.

Prices for diesel — used for agriculture, heating homes and trucking — are near record highs and could hurt Trump's fellow Republicans in next month's congressional elections that will determine whether they maintain their thin majorities in Congress.

Analysts have said Trump's agreement with Moscow was unlikely to lead to sustained lower fuel prices.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday that the Trump administration ‌will follow through with the deal using existing legal ⁠authority, adding that the agreement was good for the American people and would bring prices down.

"We're going to do it with all the legal authorities we have. So, you know, anyone in Congress who says whether it's an old bill or ⁠the current Lindsey Graham bill (that) prohibits us from doing it is wrong," Bessent told the "Fox & Friends" program.

Trump last month signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill into law, called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," to honor the South Carolina Republican who died in July. Graham, a longtime Russia hawk, was a staunch backer of ​the ​legislation.

Tillis is not the first Republican to criticize the deal. Retiring Representative Don Bacon of ​Nebraska said on X on Friday that "propping up (Russian President Vladimir) ‌Putin's war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities."

Mike Pence, Trump's former vice president, called his decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil a "betrayal" of Graham's legacy and urged the president to "rescind" it.

"The president's actions and his comments over the last 24 hours are the exact opposite of the intent of that bill," Tillis said, adding, "I will guarantee you at the first opportunity Putin has to embarrass or undermine President Trump, he will."

As Trump's poll numbers have cratered, congressional Republicans have increasingly distanced themselves from the president, on matters ranging from the conflict in Iran to the trade war with Canada.

The Senate's No. ‌2 Republican, John Barrasso of Wyoming, defended the diesel deal on Sunday, telling CBS' "Face the ​Nation" that Trump is focused on bringing costs down for consumers, ranchers, farmers and truckers.

"The ​president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said.

Canadian Prime ​Minister Mark Carney in a call on Sunday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy made it clear that the US-Russia diesel ‌deal "is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and ​our allies to create peace and stability ​in Europe," his office said in a statement.

In a social media post on Sunday, Trump claimed that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to what he described as an "energy ceasefire" that would take effect immediately, but did not elaborate.

Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details ​of the deal.

"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important ‌that Russia support it as well," Zelenskiy said in a post on the Telegram app.

But there was no word from Moscow on ​the announcement, which followed days of US pressure on Ukraine to halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
